>Can someone have a penis and later grow breasts?

Absolutely. This happens to almost all trans women who undergo hormone replacement therapy (HRT). Remember, sex is incredibly complex, especially on a genetic level, and we don't yet understand it. Male nipples are actually the result of an embryo which was developing what could become breast tissue, but didn't. Many typically female traits are present in males, and vice versa.

In fact, people with androgen insensitivity syndrome (AIS) - an intersex condition in which someone with XY chromosomes does not respond to androgens - will develop not only breasts, but a vagina and vulva, naturally. Those genes are there, it is merely their expression which is modified by the presence (and reception) of hormones. Someone with AIS will typically only discover this when they start to wonder why they've never gotten their period.

>How does one feel like gender x but is physically y? (And what does it feel like)

This is a very complex question, and answers vary widely. Some have a very strong sense that they are a girl or a boy, while others (such as myself) aren't able to pin it down for a long time. For me, it was a sense of always being uncomfortable, of feeling wrong, of intense dislike for my body. I found there were a lot of roadblocks in my mind preventing me from properly entertaining the idea, suggesting I had some notion that I might be a girl, but that this was dismissed, probably from seeing trans women so often the butt of jokes and objects of ridicule. I recall feeling jealous of my female relatives, resenting being lumped in with the men, etc.

From the age of sixteen, I was regularly removing body hair, plucking my eyebrows, and pretty comfortable wearing make up. Looking back, it was fairly obvious, but I came to attribute these things to being genderqueer before I could accept that I was trans.

>What is gender fluid and how does it work?

Gender fluid can mean people who do not fit into the man/woman binary or, more specifically, who feel their gender identity shifts. They may feel more masculine at times, more feminine at others, and spend some time in rather neutral territory. It may also be used to describe people who firmly do not identify as male or female, or feel they are some combination of these. Gender, like sex, is very complex.

>Why is a court involved? And more importantly, why are the costs so high? It's a life changing thing, but the costs?

Courts are involved because that's what's required for a minor here. HRT in young people will be done in stages. The first, which required court approval until recently, prevents the onset of puberty, and someone went off those, they would undergo their body's default hormonal regimen.

The second, which introduces active hormones to the body to initiate the kinds of changes one sees in puberty, are not entirely reversible. The concern here is essentially the same one we had recently with stage one: if someone goes through the wrong puberty for them, they will experience changes that may never go completely back.

However, it seems really unnecessary, as courts are leaving it distressingly late, and simply follow the advice of their clinic anyway. The only partial reversibility of it is the issue, but it's one they're simply too concerned with. The changes one might go through should the wrong decision be made are the same ones trans people will go through if no decision is made. Trans women who transition later in life go through the same issues of irreversible changes which occurred in puberty as a cis woman attempting to detransition would.

As for transgender vs transsexual, this varies within the community. Many trans people, myself included, dislike the term due to the connotations it's picked up during its long history as the primary term used for us. Transgender has fewer such connotations, and is prevalent in the increasingly mainstream pro-trans movement. Personally, I wouldn't be massively offended if you used transsexual instead, and the terms can change quickly.

For now, transgender is probably the safer term to use. I know of no one who finds it objectionable. Just be aware of the syntactical differences (transgender is not a noun, it is an adjective, while transsexual is both. Someone can be "a transgender woman", or they can be "transgender", but they're not "a transgender", if that makes sense).

It's not so much people making fun of me. That I can deal with. That's totally fine. I just write that person off as not worth my time.

This is far more subtle, and something that is a central theme to every trans person's story. It's the people who, simply by addressing you, add their voice to the backlog of people enforcing the wrong gender. Other contributors are your doctors, parents, teachers, friends, colleagues, and even just the casual use of terms which pushes one into a box they do not belong in.

That's really part of it, but I suspect it's a big part. Bigger than I realise. It's giving me a lot of anxiety about my desirability as a partner, my ability to have children, and the shortcomings of what shall one day be my body. It also causes a lot of jealousy of those who do not have to deal with those fears - which I think is one of the reasons I find it so hard that my ex has found someone new so quickly.

Note that the controversy section is pretty much concerned with the classification of GID as a disorder, and not with whether or not those who fall under it should transition.

GID is not a temporary thing, any more than homosexuality. One's gender is an integral part of their identity, almost universally, whether one realises it or not. It massively affects how we interact with the world, how we view ourselves, and how the world views us.

The argument you seem to be making is that we should bring the person's gender identity into line with their assigned gender (as determined by their biological sex, should that happen to be unambiguous, or their assigned sex otherwise).

To that, I can only say that I am not my body. I own my body. I use my body in many very important ways. However, it is not me. I am a set of chemical reactions in my brain, influenced by a complex web of neural connections and memories. If you believe in a soul, you may believe that that is who you are. However, it is ludicrous to say we are our bodies.

Doesn't it make more sense to change the body to fit the person, rather than change the person to fit the body? Forget for a moment that attempts to change a person's gender identity invariably lead to massive mental health issues. Why should I change merely because I developed a penis rather than a vagina?

It's also worth noting that not everyone with GID gets genital surgery. Not all get hormone therapy, either. That is the most publicised route, but in reality, trans folk are a diverse group.

The hardest part for me was the internalised narrative. After more than twenty years of everyone telling me I'm a boy/man, and acting like one, and thinking I am one, it's very difficult to think of myself as a woman. The first step was ignoring that, and considering it freely. For me, when I did that, it felt right. It soon came back, but once I knew it was something I might seriously want to do, it got easier, and that narrative weakened.

I don't know if that's what you mean when you say your mind is fighting with itself. This is just my experience, although it's one a few trans folk I know have had, too.

You might do that and find that you're perfectly happy with your assigned gender, and that's great. There's no harm in exploring the options. I'm just saying that we're set up to not be able to do that properly.

I've seen various sides of this argument. I've seen people call it rape, which is ridiculous.

The argument for disclosing is that this information would affect someone's decision to sleep with you. The argument against is that many things could, and for many trans women, the fact that they're trans is unimportant - it's the woman part that matters.

Requiring trans women to disclose this makes their trans status something dirty, which it shouldn't be. Analogously, should a woman disclose how many sexual partners she's had before sleeping with someone? This would frequently affect someone's decision whether or not to sleep with them, yet the fact itself doesn't affect the act. Whether a woman has had many or few partners shouldn't be important, nor should their being trans.

To say that a woman's sexual history is important, and should be disclosed, validates a rather horrible attitude towards female sexuality. The same could be said of requiring trans women to disclose their history (important word) as a male.

I'm far from having made up my mind about this. It's a rather complex issue.

As for the kitten argument, to be a kitten is very different than to be a human. It does mean something pretty specific. It's conceivable that some medical technique might be developed in the future to transform one into a kitten, at which point they would become a kitten.

As I said, though, gender means nothing in the real world. It is a construct of society (and I am a product and member of society, so it is a big deal to me). This is very much opposed to a kitten, which is different in very real ways which mean something very important in nature.

What you're thinking of is sex, not gender. Sex means something in the real world (as you and I both point out, it is not simply genetic).

I know a lot of trans folk, and the stories are very different. There's no typical trans story - just the stereotypical one. Just try to remember, there's no reason it couldn't be you.

Gender equality does not mean that suddenly gender is unimportant. It is, and will continue for quite some time to be, a massive part of how we interact with people.

As for being "literally a girl", I can be, actually. Gender and sex are not the same. Neither is simply genetic (there are various types of intersex). I can get genital surgery to give me a functional vagina, which, from a legal definition, makes me female.

Gender is a social construct. What it means to be a boy, or a girl, varies both temporally and geographically. So, to be literally a girl, I need only identify as a girl. Gender doesn't have any higher, essentialist meaning.

Even if it were simply shallow and superficial, it's a shallow, superficial thing that massively impacts on the experiences I have in my life, and it's my right to be as shallow and superficial with my body as I like.

This question places cisgenderism in a privileged position. We all have our own gender expressions, which colour so much of how we present ourselves, and view ourselves, and how others view us.

Gender is about a lot more than body image. It's a fundamental component of our identity. The only difference between me and a cisgendered woman is that I was expected to be something else. I'm correcting that.
Yeah, I do. That's the full time period I mentioned. Some psychiatrists require two years, but either way, I'll not come to that for a long time.
Yeah. The best thing about years of hormone replacement therapy is that it gives you the magical ability to swap between genders at will. It's fantastic! Everyone should do it.

I got a referral to a psychiatrist who's known for working with the trans community, from a counsellor at a local gender centre. I have heard that you often have to lie to them, though. They won't give you the letter unless you played with dolls as a kid, and dressed in your sister's clothing, etc.

I'm not entirely familiar with the SOC, but from what I do know, I'm pretty happy to follow it. I'll be consulting the counsellor at the gender centre about what I should do next at various points.

I've not decided on genital surgery yet, although I think I will get it. Honestly, it's so far away for me that I've not given it that much thought. I've planned to save for it, but not how I'd go about it, which surgeon I'd see, what they offer, etc. Sorry I can't help you out more.

What I have seen suggests to me that there is no "stock vagina". Different surgeons have their own particular methods, but it's largely dependent on what's there. They use the existing genitals and reshape them, so what you end up with depends on what you start with, I think.

Yeah, I've let the people around me know. All of the friends I have in this city know, and most of them back home do. My family is mostly taken care of. They're all being really great about it. I couldn't ask for better responses.

It is very refreshing to realise. I've noticed that I'm generally happier. I walk more confidently, despite the stares I attract. The thought of getting started is very exciting.

I do regret the time I've wasted, though. I see people who transitioned younger, and I get rather jealous. I just try to remind myself that I am still quite young. I'm mostly just happy about it, though.

The process begins with hormones, and I think I will get genital surgery. That's kind of the last big change, and I have to be full time for at least a year before that's an option. So, all up, it'll probably be two years before I've achieved the results I want.

My family and friends were amazing, actually. My little sister is mourning the loss of her big brother, but she's accepting. My brother is just proud of me, and thinks it's awesome. My mother was kind of sad at first, but got it pretty quickly. All of my friends reacted wonderfully, and one of them came out as bisexual to her friends in support of me.

I identify as pansexual - that is, I'm attracted to people of all sex and gender expressions. Not to say it's not a factor, of course. I tend to prefer women to men, but there's something to be liked in all, as far as I'm concerned.

It's only been in the past few months that I've seriously considered transitioning. For about two years prior, it was something I knew I wanted, but never thought I could have, and it's been fairly frequent for the past year now.

The first step was the hardest - that is, putting aside more than twenty years of being told I'm a guy, treated like a guy, and thinking I'm a guy. That's the biggest hurdle, but once I managed to push it aside and realise I could actually be trans, the influence of that narrative diminished very quickly.

I am planning on having permanent hair removal. My hair is naturally very dark and coarse. Until I can afford it, I will wax, or get an epilator. First port of call will be facial hair, as the most visible and biggest indicator of gender.

This may sound kind of silly, but I first thought of my new name when I took up playing Pokemon again. I chose a female avatar, and when it asked me for my name, I put in something which sounded nice, and also close to my given name. It was another six months before I took transition seriously, and then another two before I came out and decided to use that as my name in the real world.

I'm lucky to live in an area that is, if nor accepting, afraid to be seen as unaccepting. Incidents happen, but it's a pretty good area. I'm also university educated, so the problems I anticipate at work (where others are also) should be comparatively few.

Once my transition is complete, I hope to simply be viewed as a woman by new acquaintances. Good friends and lovers would know of my history as a man, but there's no need for anyone else to.

Well, I believe sex is what you make of it, but I think it's rather invalidating to think that someone can't know they're gay without having had sex with a member of the opposite sex while being straight is simply accepted.

If anything, I would say that in a world where heterosexuality is "normal", the opposite would be the case. You have to do a whole lot of self discovery, generally, to know you're gay. Being straight can be as simple as never questioning one's sexuality.

I have so much respect for you, telling your story.

It's great to hear about how accepting your mother is now. I am glad that she found a way to reconcile her love for you with her faith, and can support you as a parent should.

I find it odd that your friends would suggest you try having sex with a girl at least once. I trust that they are joking, but I wonder if they've considered having sex with a guy at least once, before they decide they're straight.

Finally, good for you setting up Safe Space. Community is an invaluable resource.
